title: RT and Haaretz Agree on AIPAC
subtitle: Russian state media and Israel's left-liberal newspaper both centered the same analytical frame in their Michigan primary coverage — from opposite geopolitical stakes.
body_md:
Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan's Democratic Senate primary by 0.97 percentage points — 48.48 to 47.51 — despite facing what Mother Jones described as the largest outside-spending campaign against a single congressional candidate in Democratic primary history. [Mother Jones](https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/08/michigans-primary-reckoning-for-the-democrats-donavan-mckinney-will-lawrence-abdul-el-sayed/) The Intercept calculated the composite figure at $62 million — half of it from AIPAC — giving his opponent Haley Stevens a 9-to-1 spending advantage. [The Intercept](https://theintercept.com/2026/08/05/michigan-primary-results-el-sayed-stevens-aipac/) Twenty-nine outlets across 17 countries covered the result, an unusual volume of international attention for a US Senate primary. Almost all of it was driven by two story elements: AIPAC's record spending and El-Sayed's potential to become the first Muslim US senator.

RT's headline: "Israel critic wins US Senate primary despite record AIPAC spending on rival." Haaretz's coverage: "Despite a lack of support from most of the Democratic establishment and in spite of $30 million spent against him by AIPAC — Abdul El-Sayed has secured the nomination." [RT](https://www.rt.com/news/643918-el-sayed-us-primary-israel/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=RSS) [Haaretz](https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/haaretz-today/2026-08-05/ty-article/.highlight/what-the-democrats-must-learn-from-el-sayeds-michigan-primary-win/0000019f-d27d-d04a-a3df-d6fde03c0000) Two outlets that diverge on virtually every political story, from opposite geopolitical hemispheres, both independently reached the same analytical axis: AIPAC's spending was the defining fact of the race. RT used it to amplify the narrative of US-Israel lobbying as corrosive to American democracy; Haaretz used it to mark a politically significant defeat for the pro-Israel establishment. The frame is identical. The conclusions are not. This convergence — the analysis calls it the clearest cross-bloc signal produced by any element of the story — is the structurally remarkable finding in this corpus.

The LaBSE cosine similarity between Canada and Turkey was 0.927 — the highest pairing in the corpus — reflecting a shared wire-service frame centered on progressive insurgency and party ideology. Most international outlets treated the primary as a proxy war for the Democratic Party's ideological direction. [Axios World](https://www.axios.com/2026/08/05/democrats-senate-michigan-el-sayed-stevens) [Deutsche Welle English](https://www.dw.com/en/us-abdul-el-sayed-wins-contentious-michigan-senate-primary/a-78258380?maca=en-rss-en-all-1573-rdf) Progressive US outlets framed the win as a historic defeat of a record outside-spending campaign. Conservative US outlets immediately labeled El-Sayed "far-left" and "extremist" and pivoted to general-election alarm.

The US press diverged sharply on what his identity means for November. Daily Caller documented the polling failure — pre-race surveys showed El-Sayed winning by a wide margin; he won by less than a point. Middle East Eye reported exclusively that AIPAC, having spent $30 million to defeat El-Sayed in the primary, is now considering backing Republican Mike Rogers against him in November — a move that would represent an explicit partisan crossover rather than merely an intra-Democratic intervention. [Middle East Eye](https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/after-major-upset-aipac-michigan-group-looks-back-republican-candidate-against-abdul-el-sayed) Jerusalem Post focused on Jewish Democrats' internal trilemma — support El-Sayed, abstain, or back Rogers — the only outlet to frame the primary as a reckoning for the Jewish-Democratic relationship specifically. Iranian state Tehran Times covered the race with restrained factual language, calling it "one of the most expensive and closely watched primaries in US history," conspicuously foregrounding AIPAC over Gaza rhetoric.

El Pais linked El-Sayed's win to Zohran Mamdani's New York victory as two data points in a single national progressive wave — the only outlet to provide that pattern context. [El Pais English](https://english.elpais.com/usa/2026-08-05/abdul-elsayed-progressive-candidate-in-the-michigan-democratic-primary-emerges-as-likely-winner.html) La Stampa, Italy's centre-left daily, offered the most structurally unusual interpretation: El-Sayed's victory as evidence of "dual populisms" — the US trapped between mirror-image insurgencies on left and right — a reading absent from all Anglophone coverage.

The November contest is what the corpus cannot yet describe. El-Sayed won a state Trump carried in 2024 by less than a point. AIPAC has indicated it may back his Republican opponent. The spending advantage that failed in the primary could reappear at a different scale in the general. Whether the AIPAC frame that united RT and Haaretz in August holds as the dominant international axis in November is the open question.
